notes:
I've organised these notes by verse. **One limit first:** I ran out of research tools before reaching several sites. I didn't find anything from Orthodox, Lutheran, Pentecostal-specific or prosperity/word-of-faith sources, or any NET Bible translator's notes, so those are left out. The sources I did find mostly agree. Where they part ways, it's mostly over how to translate a line, how far to read Christ into the psalm, and which historical setting it fits, not over doctrine.

---

## v. 1 (title and opening)

**Traditional reading**
- **Title.** Guzik says the title's historical notes place the psalm early in David's reign, when he was conquering his neighbours. He links it to 2 Samuel 8 and 10 and to 1 Chronicles 18, where the Valley of Salt battle against Edom appears. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-60/
- **The defeat behind the psalm.** Guzik notes that 2 Samuel and Chronicles don't mention the setbacks this psalm mourns. He takes this to mean the history books shorten events: the victories were real but didn't come all at once. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-60/
- **A possible backstory.** David Mathis (Desiring God) suggests that while Israel's army was away fighting Aram in the north, Edom invaded from the south. That would be why Joab had to "return" to fight Edom. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/fall-back-to-the-banner
- **"You have rejected us."** Guzik says David knew that when the Lord fought for Israel, victory was certain. So he took defeat as a sign of God's displeasure and appealed to that deeper cause, not just the military one. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-60/
- **Spurgeon's comment (quoted by Guzik).** Being cast off by God is the worst calamity. But when it leads to mourning and repentance, it is only partial and temporary. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-60/
- **God's control over defeat.** Mathis says real hope starts by admitting that God rules his people's losses as well as their victories. David says "You" to God over and over, but humbly, not as an accusation. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/fall-back-to-the-banner

**Catholic reading (Augustine)**
- Augustine reads the psalm with Christ and the Church as the speaker. In his view, those God "drove back and destroyed" were evil people, struck down so they could be brought back to life as good ones. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801060.htm

## v. 2

**Traditional reading**
- Guzik says David felt as if the whole earth shook at the defeat. Yet the God who can shake the earth can also heal its cracks. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-60/

**Catholic reading (Augustine)**
- Augustine takes the shaken earth to mean sinners' consciences, stirred by the call "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near" (Matthew 3:2). https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801060.htm

## v. 3

**Traditional reading**
- **"Hardship."** Guzik finds some comfort in knowing God was behind it: what God does in discipline, he can undo in love. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-60/
- **"The wine that staggers us."** Adam Clarke, quoted by Guzik, says the people reeled like drunk men from shock and dismay at their enemies' success. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-60/

## v. 4 (the most discussed verse)

**Traditional reading**
- **What the banner is.** Barnes says the Hebrew word for "banner" means anything lifted up: a flag, a sign or a signal. Here it is an army's standard, given to God's people as soldiers in his cause. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/60-4.htm
- **Spurgeon.** The banner was a rallying point, proof that God had sent them to fight, and a guarantee of victory. Those who fear God most fear people least. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/60-4.htm
- **Guzik.** Even feeling broken, David kept flying the banner of loyalty to God. He links it to the Exodus 17 story, where Moses named an altar "the Lord is my Banner." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-60/
- **Mathis.** The banner is a place to fall back to when the front line breaks. He identifies it as prayer, and more specifically as "what God has spoken" (vv. 6–8). https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/fall-back-to-the-banner

**Translation question: "flee the bow" or "because of the truth"?**
- This is the main textual issue. Older English versions read "displayed because of the truth." Ellicott says we should follow the Greek Old Testament (LXX) and read "bow" instead of "truth," with the sense of rallying out of the archers' range. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/60-4.htm
- The Cambridge Bible prefers the same ancient reading. It adds that verses 1–4 form the first stanza, which is supported by where the "Selah" falls and by Psalm 108 picking up the text at verse 5. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/60-4.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary mentions a darker version of this reading, revived by Professor Cheyne: God gave a banner, "but only that they may flee before the bow." On that view, the last time the banner went up it signalled scattering, not rallying. https://biblehub.com/psalms/60-4.htm
- Catholic translations take the same ancient line. The Douay-Rheims reads "a warning… that they may flee from before the bow." https://biblehub.com/psalms/60-4.htm

**How the traditions apply it**
- **Reformed (Calvin):** Calvin rejects reading the verse as a wish ("O that you would give a banner"). He takes it as David pointing out a change God had already made. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/60-4.html
- **Presbyterian (Matthew Henry):** The banner was David's government, set up over all Israel and welcomed by God-fearing Israelites. Ultimately Christ is the banner (Isaiah 11:10). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/60-4.html
- **Methodist (Benson):** "For those who fear you" means God gave this blessing to the whole nation for the sake of the few sincere believers in it. Christ is the banner under which believers fight the powers of darkness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/60-4.htm
- **Methodist (Clarke):** Handing over a banner may have meant a promise of protection. God had given Israel to its enemies for a time, but now showed it was under his care again. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/60-4.html
- **Baptist (Gill):** Gill gives the strongest gospel reading. The banner is the sending of Christ and the preaching of the gospel. "Truth" means God's faithfulness in keeping his promises. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/60-4.html

## v. 5

**Traditional reading**
- **"Beloved."** Guzik says David still calls himself God's beloved despite the defeat, seeing that rescue lies in more loyalty to God, not less. Kidner (quoted there) says the Hebrew word comes from love poetry. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-60/
- **Matthew Henry.** Those who fear God are his beloved, the apple of his eye, and "those that have his heart have his hand." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_060.cfm
- **Link to Psalm 108.** Smith notes that verses 5–12 are the same as Psalm 108:6–13. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/60-7.html

## v. 6

**Traditional reading**
- **Turning point.** Mathis calls this verse the hinge of the psalm: "God has spoken" changes everything. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/fall-back-to-the-banner
- **A prophet's message.** Guzik takes David as speaking like an inspired prophet, passing on God's own words. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-60/
- **Kingcomments.** This is God's answer to the prayer in verse 5. It is a solemn statement made from his sanctuary. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/psalms-60.html
- **"In his holiness" vs "from his sanctuary."** Ellicott notes the Greek and Latin versions read "in his sanctuary," which suits a word from God. He suggests "I will shout in triumph," and says "I may divide" shows unquestioned ownership. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/60-6.htm
- **Methodist (Benson):** He reads "by his holiness," like an oath, compare Psalm 89:35. God didn't just speak; he swore. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/60-6.htm
- **Shechem and Succoth.** Ellicott says they are named to mark the whole width of the land, west to east. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/60-6.htm
- **Real places, not symbols.** Guzik says the specific place names show God speaking about real geography and his special care for the land of Israel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-60/
- **Trapp.** Since God had promised these places, David already counted them as his own. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/psalms-60.html

**Catholic reading (Augustine)**
- "In his Holy One" means Christ, in whom "God was reconciling the world to himself." https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801060.htm

## v. 7

**Traditional reading**
- **The whole land.** Ellicott says Gilead and Manasseh (east of the Jordan) and Ephraim and Judah (west of it) together stand for the whole kingdom. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/60-7.htm
- **Judah the "lawgiver."** Ellicott says the Hebrew word can mean either a lawmaker or the staff or sceptre that symbolised law (Genesis 49:10). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/60-7.htm
- **Ephraim the "helmet."** Barnes says Ephraim was David's main strength, protecting him as a helmet protects the head. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/60-7.htm
- **Kidner (quoted by Guzik).** Notice the repeated "Mine": everything belongs to God, and Israel holds it as his tenants. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-60/

**How the traditions apply it**
- **Baptist (Spurgeon):** He applies "Judah is my lawgiver" against church authorities. Believers take no orders from Rome, Oxford or church councils, only from Christ, the King who came from Judah. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps060.cfm
- **Methodist (Clarke):** Unusually, Clarke links this part of the psalm to the return from Babylon, with Zerubbabel as Judah's leader. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/60-7.html
- **Older German scholarship (Delitzsch, in Keil & Delitzsch):** Calling Judah the king's sceptre shows that the king is the speaker here, not the people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/60-7.htm

## v. 8

**Traditional reading**
- **Proud nations humbled.** Guzik says Moab and Edom were known for pride, and here God gives them humble servants' jobs. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-60/
- **"Washbasin."** Benson says a washbasin was a lowly household item, used for the feet. It fits the Moabites' coming slavery (2 Samuel 8:2). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/60-8.htm
- **The sandal.** Ellicott thinks the likeliest meaning is that Edom becomes a slave who is tossed the conqueror's sandals to clean. He says Ruth 4:7, a sandal handed over to transfer ownership, is a different custom. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/60-8.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary.** It agrees the Ruth link is doubtful and notes that Balaam foretold Edom's defeat (Numbers 24:18). https://biblehub.com/psalms/60-8.htm
- **Another view.** Some other writers do take the sandal as a sign of claiming ownership. https://biblehub.com/sermons/psalms/60-8.htm
- **Calvin.** David makes a clear distinction: fellow Israelites would be ruled as brothers, while foreign enemies could be forced into submission. https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom09/calcom09.xxvi.ii.html
- **Baptist (Gill):** This came true under David (2 Samuel 8:14). Gill also applies it to the gospel spreading among the Gentiles. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/lit/psalms/60-8.html

## v. 9

**Traditional reading**
- **"The fortified city."** Boice (quoted by Guzik) identifies it as Petra, Edom's seemingly unbeatable mountain fortress. Only God could win there. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-60/
- **Mathis.** When David asks "Who?", he already knows the answer, because he has just repeated God's word to himself. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/fall-back-to-the-banner

## v. 10

**Traditional reading**
- Guzik says David knew the earlier defeat came because God didn't go out with the armies, and trusted God to lead them now. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-60/
- Matthew Henry reads it as an appeal to God's promise: God has spoken in his holiness, so surely he'll keep his word. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_060.cfm

**Catholic reading (Augustine)**
- The God who drove them back is the very one who will lead them. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801060.htm

## v. 11

**Traditional reading**
- **Trapp.** Israel had just learned this from Saul, the king they chose, who couldn't save them from the Philistines. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-60/
- **VanGemeren.** David isn't looking for a military fix such as alliances with other kings. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-60/

**Catholic reading (Augustine)**
- Help comes from the very place where God seemed to have left them. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801060.htm

## v. 12

**Traditional reading**
- **Spurgeon (quoted by Guzik).** God's working is no excuse for doing nothing; it's the best encouragement to brave effort. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-60/
- **Matthew Henry.** Trusting God should drive our efforts, not replace them. Hope in God is the best basis for courage. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_060.cfm
- **Mathis.** Note the order: "we" act, "he" tramples. We act in faith, but God's action decides the outcome. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/fall-back-to-the-banner
